title: LRU Cache
prompt:
Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with a fixed positive `capacity`. It should support `get(key)`, which returns the value for `key` if present (or `-1` otherwise) and marks the key as most recently used, and `put(key, value)`, which inserts or updates the value for `key`, marking it as most recently used; if adding a new key would exceed capacity, the least recently used key must be evicted first. Both operations must run in O(1) average time.

You'll implement this as a single function `runLruOps(capacity, ops)`, where `ops` is an array of `[operationName, args...]` entries applied in order to one cache instance of the given capacity: `["put", key, value]` (no output) and `["get", key]` (pushes its return value onto the output array). Return the output array. A doubly linked list combined with a hash map of key -> node is the classic way to get O(1) access, move-to-front, and eviction all at once.

examples.explanation: Capacity 2: after put(1,1) and put(2,2), get(1) returns 1 and marks 1 as most recent. put(3,3) evicts key 2 (least recently used). get(2) returns -1. put(4,4) evicts key 1. get(1)=-1, get(3)=3, get(4)=4.

constraints: At most 2 * 10^4 total calls to get and put
hints: A plain dict alone gives O(1) lookup but no way to cheaply track or update recency order — you need an ordering structure alongside it.
A doubly linked list lets you remove any node in O(1) once you have a reference to it (no need to search), which is exactly what a hash map of key -> node gives you.

Keep the list ordered from least-recently-used (near one sentinel/dummy end) to most-recently-used (near the other). Every get or put on an existing key removes that node from its current position and reinserts it at the most-recently-used end; put on a new key at full capacity removes the node at the least-recently-used end before inserting.

solution.approach: Maintain a hash map from key to a doubly linked list node holding (key, value), plus two sentinel nodes marking the least-recently-used end and most-recently-used end of the list. Both get and put on an existing key unlink that node and reinsert it right before the most-recently-used sentinel (O(1) since we already have the node reference from the map). put on a new key creates a node, inserts it at the most-recently-used end, and — if this pushes the map over capacity — removes the node right after the least-recently-used sentinel (the true LRU entry) from both the list and the map. Every operation touches a fixed number of pointers and one hash map lookup, giving O(1) average time.
